title: Congenital Heart Conditions
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the congenital heart conditions most often tested: ventricular and atrial septal defects, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and transposition of the great vessels. Each is taught from its embryologic origin to the pressures and resistances that set shunt direction, then to the murmur, the pulse findings, cyanosis, and late complications such as Eisenmenger syndrome. Board questions usually give a murmur, a pulse or saturation pattern, a chest film, or a syndrome and ask you to name the lesion or predict its course. If you can say which side has the higher pressure and which chambers carry the extra volume, most of these questions answer themselves.
prerequisites: Cardiac septation, endocardial cushions, and the spiral aorticopulmonary septum (CV-1)
Fetal circulation and the changes at birth (CV-1)
Pressures in each cardiac chamber and the cardiac cycle with heart sounds
Flow, pressure, and resistance (Poiseuille relationship) and the causes of turbulence (CV-11)
Oxygen content, hemoglobin saturation, and the Fick principle

connections.how: Each defect here is a specific failure of septation, cushion fusion, conotruncal spiraling, or ductal closure described in the embryology chapter.
Eisenmenger syndrome is pulmonary arterial hypertension caused by chronic shunt flow, with the same endothelial imbalance and plexiform lesions.
Bicuspid aortic valve is a leading cause of aortic stenosis and regurgitation in younger adults, and turbulent jets from shunts and abnormal valves seed endocarditis.
Trisomy 21, 22q11.2 deletion, Turner syndrome, maternal diabetes, and congenital rubella each predict a particular lesion.
Chronic hypoxemia drives erythropoietin and secondary polycythemia, and right-to-left shunts let venous clots and bacteria reach the brain.

terms.def: Abnormal flow of blood between the systemic and pulmonary circulations through a defect in a septum or a persistent vessel.
The ratio of pulmonary blood flow to systemic blood flow; above 1 means a net left-to-right shunt, below 1 a net right-to-left shunt.
Bluish skin and mucosa that appears when capillary blood contains about 5 g/dL or more of deoxygenated hemoglobin.
Reversal of a long-standing left-to-right shunt to right-to-left after pulmonary vascular disease raises right-sided pressure above left-sided pressure.
Resistance of the pulmonary arterioles to flow; high in the fetus, it falls sharply after birth and rises again with shunt-induced vascular disease.
Passage of a venous thrombus from the right heart to the systemic arteries through an intracardiac defect, causing stroke or limb ischemia.
Swellings of the atrioventricular canal that fuse to divide it into right and left channels and contribute to the membranous septum, the lower atrial septum, and the AV valves.
The smooth-walled outflow tract of the right ventricle leading to the pulmonary valve, also called the conus arteriosus.
A widely split second heart sound whose aortic and pulmonic components stay apart in both inspiration and expiration, typical of atrial septal defect.
Cyanosis of the lower body with pink upper extremities, caused by deoxygenated blood entering the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.
A defect in which survival depends on flow through the ductus arteriosus, so the infant deteriorates when the ductus closes.

blocks.text: Blood crossing a defect moves toward the side with lower pressure or, for defects between filling chambers, toward the side that fills more easily. After birth the left side runs at systemic pressures (left ventricle about 120/10 mmHg) and the right side at pulmonary pressures (right ventricle about 25/5 mmHg), so a ventricular septal defect (VSD), an atrial septal defect (ASD), or a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) sends oxygenated blood back to the lungs. Systemic arterial blood is still fully saturated, so the child is not cyanotic. The cost is volume: the lungs and the chambers carrying the recirculated blood receive more flow than the body uses, expressed as a Qp:Qs ratio above 1.

Fetal pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high and falls over the first several weeks after birth. A large VSD or PDA therefore causes few symptoms at birth, then shunts more and causes heart failure within the first one to two months. The location of the shunt also decides what the pulmonary arteries face. A defect before the tricuspid valve (ASD) adds flow at low pressure, while a defect after it (VSD, PDA) transmits systemic pressure as well as extra flow, so pulmonary vascular disease develops earlier and more often with VSD and PDA.

Chronic high flow and pressure injure the pulmonary endothelium. Nitric oxide and prostacyclin fall, endothelin-1 rises, and the arterioles undergo medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation and fibrosis, and finally plexiform lesions, the same changes seen in pulmonary arterial hypertension (CV-18-A). As PVR rises, the right ventricle hypertrophies, the shunt shrinks, then becomes bidirectional, and finally reverses when right-sided pressure exceeds left-sided pressure. Advanced remodeling is irreversible.

blocks.title: From left-to-right shunt to Eisenmenger syndrome
steps: Left-to-right shunt overloads the pulmonary circulation
High flow and pressure injure pulmonary endothelium
Medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions raise PVR
Right ventricle hypertrophies as its pressure rises
Right pressure exceeds left; shunt reverses
Late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia
blocks.caption: Eisenmenger syndrome is the end stage of an uncorrected left-to-right shunt; the reversal follows years of pulmonary vascular remodeling.

blocks.text: Each Eisenmenger finding follows from the reversal. Deoxygenated blood enters the systemic arteries, so cyanosis appears late and does not correct with supplemental oxygen, because the shunted blood never passes the alveoli. Renal hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia, which raises viscosity and makes cyanosis more visible. Clubbing accompanies chronic hypoxemia; a leading explanation is that platelet clumps bypass the pulmonary capillaries and release growth factors in the fingertips. The right ventricle hypertrophies, P2 becomes loud, and the original murmur softens as the pressure difference across the defect disappears.

blocks.title: Shunt categories
rows: Hypoxemia plus right ventricular pressure overload
blocks.caption: Shunt direction, not the defect itself, determines whether the patient is cyanotic.

blocks.title: Estimating Qp:Qs from oxygen saturations
blocks.text: By the Fick principle, Qp:Qs = (systemic arterial minus mixed venous saturation) divided by (pulmonary venous minus pulmonary arterial saturation). A child with a VSD has systemic arterial saturation 98%, superior vena cava saturation 70%, pulmonary venous saturation 98%, and pulmonary arterial saturation 85%. Qp:Qs = (98 minus 70) divided by (98 minus 85) = 28 divided by 13, about 2.2, a large shunt. The step up in saturation from the vena cava to the pulmonary artery is the shunted oxygenated blood; with no step up, Qp:Qs would be 1.

Ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart defect at birth when bicuspid aortic valve is not counted. The interventricular septum has a thick muscular part and a small membranous part just below the aortic valve. The membranous septum forms last, from fusion of the endocardial cushions, the conotruncal ridges, and the muscular septum, so it is the part most often left incomplete; most VSDs are membranous or perimembranous. Muscular defects lie within the trabeculated septum and may be multiple. VSD is associated with trisomy 21, fetal alcohol exposure, and other chromosomal syndromes, and it is one of the four components of tetralogy of Fallot.

Left ventricular pressure exceeds right ventricular pressure from the start of isovolumetric contraction until the end of ejection, so blood crosses the defect throughout systole. That produces a harsh holosystolic murmur, starting with S1 and often obscuring it, loudest at the left lower sternal border (third and fourth intercostal spaces), frequently with a thrill. Raising systemic resistance, as with sustained handgrip, increases the left-to-right gradient and makes the murmur louder.

The shunted blood leaves the left ventricle during systole and passes almost directly into the pulmonary artery, so the volume load falls on the pulmonary circulation, the left atrium, and the left ventricle. That is why a large VSD enlarges the left atrium and left ventricle, while the right ventricle enlarges mainly when pulmonary pressure rises.

blocks.title: Small versus large VSD
rows: Small; RV pressure approaches LV pressure
Softer or shorter; apical mid-diastolic rumble from high mitral flow; loud P2
Set by PVR versus systemic resistance
Often closes spontaneously; endocarditis risk if it persists
Heart failure in the first months; Eisenmenger if uncorrected
blocks.caption: Murmur loudness reflects the pressure gradient, not defect size, so the loudest VSDs are often the smallest.

blocks.text: Many small defects, especially muscular ones, close spontaneously during early childhood as surrounding muscle grows or as tricuspid septal leaflet tissue covers a perimembranous opening. A large defect allows ventricular pressures to equalize, so the size of the shunt is set by the ratio of pulmonary to systemic resistance. As PVR falls over the first weeks, pulmonary flow rises and left heart volume overload produces heart failure: tachypnea, sweating and fatigue with feeds, poor weight gain, and hepatomegaly. Without correction, pulmonary vascular disease can become irreversible within the first few years of life, and Eisenmenger reversal follows. A defect just below the aortic valve can let an aortic cusp prolapse into it, adding aortic regurgitation, and the high-velocity jet damages the right ventricular endocardium where it strikes, creating a site for endocarditis.

sections.title: Atrial septal defects and patent foramen ovale

blocks.text: The atrial septum forms from two overlapping partitions (CV-1). The septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, closing the ostium primum, while perforations in its upper part create the ostium secundum. The thicker septum secundum then grows on its right side, leaving an opening, the foramen ovale, whose flap valve is the septum primum. In the fetus, high right atrial pressure pushes the flap open; after birth, left atrial pressure rises above right and presses the flap shut, and the two septa usually fuse over the following months.

blocks.title: Defects of the atrial septum
rows: Excess resorption of septum primum or a septum secundum too small to cover the ostium secundum; true tissue deficit at the fossa ovalis
Most common ASD; fetal alcohol exposure, Holt-Oram syndrome (upper limb defects); ECG right axis deviation and incomplete RBBB
Septum primum fails to meet the endocardial cushions; a partial atrioventricular septal defect
Trisomy 21; usually a cleft anterior mitral leaflet with mitral regurgitation; ECG left (superior) axis deviation
Septum primum and septum secundum fail to fuse; no tissue is missing, the flap is simply unsealed
Present in about one in four adults; no shunt while left atrial pressure exceeds right
blocks.caption: An ASD is missing septal tissue; a patent foramen ovale is complete tissue that never sealed.

blocks.text: Left atrial pressure is only a few mmHg above right, so an ASD shunts left to right mainly because the thin-walled right ventricle is more compliant and fills more easily than the left. Flow across the defect itself is low velocity and silent. The extra volume passes through the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary arteries, enlarging them, while the left atrium decompresses through the defect. The resulting increased flow across a normal pulmonic valve produces a systolic ejection (flow) murmur at the left upper sternal border, and a large shunt adds a mid-diastolic rumble from increased tricuspid flow.

Normally inspiration increases venous return to the right heart and delays pulmonic valve closure, so S2 splits in inspiration and narrows in expiration. In an ASD the right ventricle already carries a large stroke volume in both phases. In inspiration the extra systemic venous return is offset by less left-to-right shunting; in expiration the shunt grows again. Right ventricular volume, and therefore the delay of P2, stays nearly constant, giving a wide, fixed split S2.

Many ASDs cause few symptoms until adulthood, when right atrial stretch produces atrial fibrillation or flutter, exercise intolerance, right heart failure, or, in a minority, Eisenmenger syndrome. Any atrial communication can briefly reverse when right atrial pressure exceeds left, as during release of a Valsalva maneuver, coughing, straining, or acute pulmonary embolism. A deep vein thrombus can then cross to the left atrium and cause a stroke or limb ischemia: a paradoxical embolism. This is why an unexplained stroke in a young adult raises suspicion of a PFO or ASD.

blocks.predict: Why does a patent foramen ovale cause no murmur and no volume overload, yet still allow a paradoxical embolism?
blocks.explain: While left atrial pressure exceeds right, the septum primum flap is held against the septum secundum and no blood crosses. It opens only when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left, which is exactly when a venous clot can pass right to left.

blocks.text: The ductus arteriosus develops from the distal part of the left sixth aortic arch. It joins the pulmonary trunk near its bifurcation, at the root of the left pulmonary artery, to the aortic arch just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. In the fetus, pulmonary vascular resistance is high, so most right ventricular output bypasses the lungs through the ductus into the descending aorta. Its smooth muscle is held relaxed by low fetal oxygen tension and by prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), produced by the placenta and the ductus and poorly cleared by the unventilated fetal lungs.

blocks.title: Closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth
steps: First breaths expand the lungs; PVR falls
Arterial PO2 rises and constricts ductal smooth muscle
Placenta removed; perfused lungs clear PGE2
Ductus closes functionally within the first few days
Intimal proliferation and fibrosis form the ligamentum arteriosum
blocks.caption: Rising oxygen and falling PGE2 act together; a ductus that misses either signal can stay open.

blocks.text: Prematurity is the major risk factor because immature ductal muscle constricts weakly to oxygen and remains sensitive to PGE2. Congenital rubella, especially from first trimester infection, causes PDA together with cataracts and sensorineural deafness, and birth at high altitude, where arterial PO2 is low, also predisposes. Prostaglandin dependence is confirmed pharmacologically: cyclooxygenase inhibition lowers PGE2 and promotes closure, whereas exogenous prostaglandin E1 holds the ductus open.

After birth, aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary arterial pressure in both systole and diastole, so blood flows from aorta to pulmonary artery throughout the cycle. The result is a continuous machine-like murmur, loudest below the left clavicle (left infraclavicular area) and peaking around S2. Because the aorta drains into the low-resistance pulmonary circuit during diastole, diastolic pressure falls, and the extra left ventricular stroke volume raises systolic pressure, giving a wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses. As with a VSD, the recirculated blood returns to the left atrium and left ventricle, so they dilate and a large PDA causes heart failure. In a premature infant whose PVR is still high, the diastolic gradient may be small and the murmur only systolic.

An uncorrected large PDA leads to pulmonary vascular disease and Eisenmenger reversal. Deoxygenated pulmonary arterial blood then enters the aorta beyond the left subclavian artery, so the lower body receives desaturated blood while the head and arms are supplied from vessels proximal to the ductus. The result is differential cyanosis: cyanotic, clubbed toes with pink fingers. Other complications are infective endarteritis at the ductal jet and, rarely, ductal aneurysm. Anatomically, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the ligamentum arteriosum, which is why surgery in this region can cause hoarseness.

blocks.predict: In a PDA with Eisenmenger syndrome, which limbs have the lower oxygen saturation, and why are the arms spared?
blocks.explain: The legs. The ductus joins the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, so reversed flow mixes only into the descending aorta; the brachiocephalic trunk and left subclavian artery receive left ventricular blood that has not been diluted.
blocks.check: The anatomy of the ductus in the first paragraph and the Eisenmenger paragraph.

blocks.text: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect. Its four features arise from one developmental error: anterosuperior (and leftward) displacement of the infundibular (outlet) septum. The displaced septum crowds the right ventricular outflow tract, producing infundibular pulmonary stenosis, often with a small pulmonary valve and arteries. Because it no longer lines up with the muscular septum, it leaves a large malalignment VSD, and the aortic root, shifted rightward, sits above that defect (overriding aorta). Right ventricular hypertrophy is the consequence, since the right ventricle pumps against the obstruction at systemic pressure through the unrestrictive VSD.

Neural crest cells migrate into the conotruncal ridges and help build the outflow septum. That explains the link with 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome), which also causes thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia and is associated with truncus arteriosus and interrupted aortic arch. Trisomy 21 and fetal alcohol exposure are other associations.

With a large VSD the two ventricles share one pressure, so where right ventricular blood goes depends on the ratio of outflow tract resistance to systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Severe stenosis diverts deoxygenated blood across the VSD into the aorta, causing early cyanosis; mild stenosis gives a balanced or even left-to-right shunt and little cyanosis. The degree of outflow obstruction therefore sets how blue the child is. The VSD is silent because there is no pressure gradient across it. The murmur is a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from flow through the narrowed outflow tract, and S2 is single because P2 is soft. Pulmonary blood flow is reduced, so Eisenmenger physiology does not develop.

On the chest film the hypertrophied right ventricle lifts the apex, and the small main pulmonary artery leaves a concave upper left heart border, giving a boot-shaped heart with reduced pulmonary vascular markings; a right-sided aortic arch is common. Chronic hypoxemia causes clubbing and secondary polycythemia, and the right-to-left shunt allows paradoxical emboli and brain abscess.

blocks.title: Hypercyanotic (tet) spell
steps: Crying, feeding, or dehydration; outflow narrows or SVR falls
More right-to-left flow across the VSD
Arterial PO2 falls; metabolic acidosis develops
Hyperpnea increases systemic venous return to the RV
Acidosis lowers SVR further; shunt increases again
blocks.caption: Each turn of the loop sends more right ventricular output to the aorta and less to the lungs; raising SVR breaks the cycle.

blocks.text: During a spell the child becomes deeply cyanotic and hyperpneic, and the outflow murmur softens or disappears because less blood crosses the obstructed outflow tract. Squatting kinks the femoral arteries and raises SVR, so more right ventricular output is pushed through the pulmonary outflow; it also briefly reduces return of desaturated blood from the legs. The knee-chest position in an infant works the same way.

blocks.title: Why squatting helps and exertion hurts
blocks.text: The right ventricle has two exits: the stenotic pulmonary outflow (fixed high resistance) and the VSD into the aorta (resistance equal to SVR). Flow divides in inverse proportion to resistance. During exercise, muscle arteriolar dilation lowers SVR, so a larger share of right ventricular output takes the aortic exit and saturation falls. Squatting raises SVR, so the share sent to the lungs rises and saturation improves. The same logic predicts that fever or a hot bath, which lower SVR, worsen cyanosis.

Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly, present in about 1 to 2% of people and more often in males. The valve forms from cushion tissue in the outflow tract; when two of the three cusps fail to separate, usually the right and left coronary cusps, the valve has two unequal leaflets, often with a raphe (ridge) marking the fused commissure. Most cases are sporadic, but it clusters in families, and some familial cases involve NOTCH1 mutations. It is common in Turner syndrome (45,X) and in coarctation of the aorta, and the three conditions form a classic triad on examinations.

Two cusps must fold and crease more than three to open fully, and they open to an eccentric, often domed orifice with turbulent flow. Repeated mechanical stress injures the leaflet endothelium and starts the same process that causes age-related calcific aortic stenosis: lipid infiltration, chronic inflammation, transformation of valve interstitial cells toward an osteoblast-like phenotype, and dystrophic calcification. In a bicuspid valve this proceeds faster, so significant stenosis typically appears one to two decades earlier, often between the 40s and 60s instead of the 70s or 80s for a normal three-cusp valve. The findings of aortic stenosis are covered in CV-18-D. A specific clue is an early systolic ejection click from the domed valve snapping open, heard while the leaflets are still mobile and lost as they calcify.

The same valve can also leak. A larger fused cusp may prolapse, or a dilated root may pull the commissures apart, so aortic regurgitation is more typical in younger patients and stenosis in older ones. Damaged leaflet surfaces and turbulent jets favor platelet and fibrin deposits that circulating bacteria can colonize, so infective endocarditis is more frequent than with a normal valve.

The ascending aorta is often abnormal too. The media shows smooth muscle loss and elastic fiber fragmentation, an intrinsic wall weakness that accompanies the valve defect and can be present even when the valve works normally, and the eccentric jet adds focal wall stress. The ascending aorta may dilate into an aneurysm, and the risk of aortic dissection is higher than in the general population, especially when Turner syndrome or coarctation coexists.

blocks.title: Complications of bicuspid aortic valve and their mechanisms
rows: Abnormal leaflet stress accelerates inflammatory calcification
Cusp prolapse or root dilation prevents coaptation
Endothelial injury from turbulent flow allows bacterial seeding
Intrinsic medial weakness plus eccentric jet stress
blocks.caption: One structural defect explains four distinct complications, so a single patient may develop several over a lifetime.

blocks.text: Coarctation of the aorta is a localized narrowing, almost always at the junction with the ductus arteriosus or ligamentum arteriosum (juxtaductal), just distal to the left subclavian artery. A leading explanation is that ductal tissue extends into the aortic wall and constricts along with the ductus after birth. It is more common in males, occurs in a substantial minority of girls with Turner syndrome, and is accompanied by a bicuspid aortic valve in most patients.

Two presentations follow from where the narrowing sits and how severe it is. A severe narrowing, often with arch hypoplasia (historically called infantile or preductal), leaves the lower body dependent on right ventricular blood flowing through the PDA, which causes lower body cyanosis. When the ductus closes in the first weeks, perfusion of the lower body and kidneys collapses, producing shock, acidosis, and absent femoral pulses. A milder narrowing (historically adult or postductal) allows time for collateral vessels to develop, and the patient may be detected only in childhood or adulthood because of hypertension.

The narrowing is a high resistance in series with everything downstream. Pressure upstream rises, so the arms, supplied by vessels arising proximal to the coarctation, are hypertensive. Pressure and flow beyond it are reduced, so femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulse (radiofemoral delay), leg blood pressure is lower than arm pressure (normally it is slightly higher), and the legs may be cool or claudicate with exercise. Reduced renal perfusion pressure activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which adds to the hypertension. The left ventricle hypertrophies against the high afterload, and long-standing hypertension proximal to the narrowing raises the risk of heart failure, aortic dissection, and rupture of cerebral berry aneurysms, which are associated with coarctation.

blocks.title: Collateral flow around a coarctation
steps: Subclavian artery above the coarctation
Internal thoracic artery
Anterior intercostal arteries
Posterior intercostal arteries, flow reversed
Descending aorta below the coarctation
blocks.caption: Chronically high collateral flow enlarges the posterior intercostal arteries, which erode the lower rib margins.

blocks.text: The enlarged, tortuous posterior intercostal arteries run in the costal grooves and erode the inferior margins of the ribs, producing rib notching on the chest film, usually from about the third rib downward. The first two ribs are spared because their intercostal arteries arise from the costocervical trunk rather than the aorta. Notching takes years to appear and is rarely seen in young children. The coarctation itself and its indented contour, with dilation above and below, may form a figure 3 sign, and flow through the narrowing and collaterals produces a systolic or continuous murmur heard over the back between the scapulae.

Normally neural crest cells form a pair of conotruncal ridges that grow in a spiral, so the aorticopulmonary septum twists about 180 degrees and connects the aorta to the left ventricle and the pulmonary trunk to the right ventricle. In transposition of the great vessels, the septum grows straight instead of spiraling. The aorta arises from the right ventricle, usually anterior and to the right, and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle. Maternal diabetes before conception is a recognized risk factor, and the lesion is more common in males.

The result is two parallel circulations instead of two in series. Systemic venous blood returns to the right atrium and right ventricle and is pumped back out the aorta to the body without being oxygenated. Pulmonary venous blood returns to the left atrium and left ventricle and is pumped back to the lungs. The left-sided circuit is highly saturated but useless to the tissues, while the aortic blood is deeply desaturated.

blocks.title: Parallel circulations in transposition
steps: Body to right atrium and right ventricle
Right ventricle to aorta, back to body
Lungs to left atrium and left ventricle
Left ventricle to pulmonary artery, back to lungs
Survival requires mixing through PFO or ASD, PDA, or VSD
blocks.caption: Without a connection between the two loops, oxygenated blood never reaches the systemic arteries.

blocks.text: Life is possible only if blood crosses between the two circuits, and the crossing must go both ways so that volume entering one circuit is returned. In the fetus this causes little difficulty, because oxygen comes from the placenta and the foramen ovale and ductus are open. After birth, an infant with an intact ventricular septum depends on a foramen ovale or ASD and a PDA. Severe cyanosis appears within hours to days and worsens as the ductus closes, and anything that keeps the ductus open or enlarges the atrial opening improves mixing. A large VSD allows more mixing, so cyanosis is milder, but pulmonary overcirculation brings early heart failure. Untreated, most infants die within the first months of life.

Supplemental oxygen raises the saturation only slightly, because it oxygenates blood that simply recirculates through the lungs. Transposition is the most common cause of cyanosis that appears on the first day of life, whereas tetralogy of Fallot is the more common cyanotic lesion overall. Because the great arteries lie front to back, the shadow of the upper mediastinum is narrow, and with a rounded heart this gives the egg-on-a-string appearance on the chest film.

blocks.title: The two classic cyanotic lesions compared
rows: Within hours to days of birth
Egg on a string, narrow mediastinum
blocks.caption: Both are conotruncal defects of outflow tract septation, but they cause cyanosis by different mechanisms.

blocks.predict: An infant with transposition and an intact ventricular septum becomes much bluer on day 3. What changed, and why does more inspired oxygen barely help?
blocks.explain: The ductus arteriosus is closing, removing one of the only mixing sites. Extra oxygen only raises saturation in the pulmonary loop, which recirculates to the lungs; it reaches the aorta only through whatever mixing remains.

integration.text: Embryology predicts the lesion and genetics predicts the embryology. Endocardial cushion failure explains ostium primum ASD and atrioventricular septal defects in trisomy 21; neural crest failure in the conotruncal ridges explains tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, and interrupted arch in 22q11.2 deletion, and failed spiraling of the same septum gives transposition; disordered outflow cushion and aortic wall development links bicuspid valve, coarctation, and aortic dilation in Turner syndrome. Teratogens act during cardiogenesis in weeks 3 to 8, so first trimester rubella, maternal diabetes, and alcohol carry the greatest risk.

Physiology and pathology then predict the course. Shunt direction follows pressure and compliance, murmurs follow gradients, chamber enlargement follows where the extra volume travels, and cyanosis follows any route that lets venous blood bypass the lungs. Pathology adds the late picture: pulmonary vascular remodeling, endocarditis on turbulent jets, dystrophic calcification, and medial degeneration of the aorta. The limits of this reasoning matter too. Many patients have more than one defect, the same lesion can be silent or severe depending on its size, and findings change with age as PVR falls in infancy and rises again with vascular disease.

summary: Shunt direction depends on pressure or compliance; after birth the left side is higher, so VSD, ASD, and PDA shunt left to right without early cyanosis.
Eisenmenger syndrome: chronic shunt flow remodels pulmonary arterioles, PVR rises, the shunt reverses, and late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia, and RVH follow.
VSD, usually membranous, gives a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; small defects are loud and often close, large ones cause heart failure as PVR falls.
Secundum ASD is most common; primum ASD is an endocardial cushion defect of trisomy 21; PFO is unfused but complete tissue. ASD gives a fixed split S2 and a pulmonic flow murmur.
Any atrial communication can allow paradoxical embolism when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left.
PDA, from the sixth arch, persists with prematurity and congenital rubella; it gives a continuous machine-like murmur, bounding pulses, and with Eisenmenger, blue toes and pink fingers.
Tetralogy of Fallot stems from anterosuperior infundibular septum displacement; outflow obstruction sets cyanosis, and squatting raises SVR to push blood to the lungs.
Bicuspid aortic valve calcifies early and also causes regurgitation, endocarditis, and ascending aortic aneurysm or dissection; it clusters with Turner syndrome and coarctation.
Coarctation raises arm pressure, weakens and delays femoral pulses, and drives intercostal collaterals that notch the ribs.
Transposition creates parallel circulations; survival depends on two-way mixing through a PFO or ASD, PDA, or VSD.

The age at which bicuspid valves typically become significantly stenotic is quoted variously from the 40s to the 60s; confirm the range NABNE expects.

Frequency of coarctation in Turner syndrome, of bicuspid valve in coarctation, and of right aortic arch in tetralogy of Fallot (often quoted near 25%) varies between sources and is stated qualitatively here.
The range of ribs showing notching in coarctation is usually given as the third to eighth or ninth ribs; confirm the version NABNE expects.
